title: Davao City did not receive ‘zero national funding’ under Marcos
claim: Davao City received no national-government funding for four years under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

sections.heading: The FMB verdict
sections.body: False. The broad claim that Davao City received no national-government funding is contradicted by official budget records. The 2026 General Appropriations Act lists multiple nationally funded road projects located in Davao City, and the Department of Budget and Management separately identified a 2026 allocation for the Davao City Bypass Construction Project.

sections.heading: What the official records show
sections.body: The FY 2026 General Appropriations Act lists four Davao City road projects under Region XI with appropriations of ₱164.727 million, ₱144.186 million, ₱144.186 million and ₱96.124 million. DBM also announced an approved allocation of ₱288.371 million for the Davao City Bypass Construction Project among infrastructure releases in 2026. These records are enough to disprove an absolute claim that the city received zero national-government funding.

sections.heading: The important distinction
sections.body: Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte later clarified that he was referring to budget allocations for congressional districts, not the National Tax Allotment automatically due to local governments. That narrower dispute is different from the viral claim that Davao City received no national funding at all. This fact check does not treat the existence of NTA or other national projects as proof that every congressional district received a separate district allocation.

sections.heading: FMB bottom line
sections.body: The viral zero-funding claim is false. Official national budget documents identify funded projects in Davao City. A separate claim about congressional-district allocations requires its own evidence and should not be conflated with the broader zero-funding statement.

title: ICC judges have not moved to end Rodrigo Duterte’s case
claim: A majority of International Criminal Court judges rejected the evidence against former president Rodrigo Duterte and moved to end his trial before the end of 2026.

sections.heading: The FMB verdict
sections.body: False. The International Criminal Court’s current case record says the opposite: all three charges were unanimously confirmed on April 23, 2026, Duterte was committed to trial, and the opening of the trial is scheduled for November 30, 2026.

sections.heading: What the ICC record says
sections.body: The ICC states that Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously confirmed three counts of crimes against humanity against Duterte after the February 2026 confirmation-of-charges hearing. The case was then committed to a Trial Chamber. The Court’s current case page continues to list November 30, 2026 as the scheduled opening of trial.

sections.heading: What the circulating claim gets wrong
sections.body: The online graphic turns litigation over evidence and pre-trial procedure into a supposed judicial decision ending the case. No such termination appears in the ICC’s official case record. Pending motions can still be decided, but that is not the same as judges having already rejected the evidence and ended the trial.

sections.heading: FMB bottom line
sections.body: As of September 16, 2026, the official ICC record shows an active case with three confirmed charges and a trial opening scheduled for November 30. The claim that ICC judges moved to end Duterte’s trial is false.

title: Lifting Sara Duterte’s arrest warrant did not dismiss her grave threats case
claim: The lifting of Vice President Sara Duterte’s arrest warrant meant she had been cleared of the grave threats case against her.

sections.heading: The FMB verdict
sections.body: Misleading. The Quezon City court lifted Duterte’s arrest warrant after she posted bail. That action released her from the warrant’s custody requirement; it did not dismiss the three grave threats charges.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 issued an arrest warrant after finding probable cause to hold Duterte for trial on three counts of grave threats. Bail was set at ₱120,000 per count. On September 5, Duterte posted bail and the court lifted the warrant.

sections.heading: Why bail is not dismissal
sections.body: Rule 114 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure defines bail as security for the release of a person in custody, conditioned on appearance before the court. The rule states that the bail undertaking remains effective through the stages of the case until promulgation of judgment, unless cancelled. Posting bail therefore does not by itself erase the criminal information or amount to an acquittal.

sections.heading: The case continued
sections.body: The distinction is confirmed by what happened next. Duterte’s arraignment remained on the court calendar and was later postponed on September 11 while her camp pursued motions challenging the proceedings. That is an ongoing case, not a dismissed one.

sections.heading: FMB bottom line
sections.body: The warrant was lifted because bail was posted. The grave threats case was not dismissed on that basis. Presenting the lifted warrant as proof that Duterte was cleared leaves out decisive context.
